It uses a circular 384,400 km orbit, 27.321661-day period and 5.145° inclination; the phase is illustrative. These scales are documented in NASA's Moon fact sheet. Earth and Moon offsets preserve the model Earth–Moon barycentre. Eccentricity, precession, perturbations and other moons are omitted. The Earth & Moon close-up resolves a lunar path that is nearly indistinguishable from Earth's on the all-planet Galactic scale.

Exterior spherical spacetime, with explicit clock references

Space & Time now offers a textured 3D Earth/body, an inverse-square field display, and an exterior Schwarzschild spatial slice. The circular-clock mode includes gravity and ideal orbital motion. Let μ=GM\mu=GM, rs=2μ/c2r_s=2\mu/c^2, and r be the areal radius outside the body's surface. For an isolated nonrotating spherical body:

(dτdt)held=1−2μrc2,(dτdt)circular=1−3μrc2,T=2πr3μ.\left(\frac{d\tau}{dt}\right)_{\rm held}=\sqrt{1-\frac{2\mu}{rc^2}},\qquad \left(\frac{d\tau}{dt}\right)_{\rm circular}=\sqrt{1-\frac{3\mu}{rc^2}},\qquad T=2\pi\sqrt{\frac{r^3}{\mu}}.

Here t is the Schwarzschild time referenced to infinity; a held clock needs support. A circular geodesic clock is in free fall even though the displayed Newtonian field magnitude is nonzero. Rates relative to a stationary surface clock use the ratio of the two lapse factors, not the difference of potentials alone. The local animation clock spans 24 hours; its acceleration setting specifies physical seconds per playback second. It is separate from the Galactic and century clocks.

For a spherical, nonrotating Earth, the 400 km circular preset has an approximately 92.4-minute period and −24.7 microseconds/day relative to the stationary surface clock. The 20,200 km preset gives +38.5 microseconds/day. This reproduces the scale and sign of the familiar GNSS result described by NIST; it is not a navigation-grade GPS correction. Earth's rotation, oblateness, other bodies, eccentricity and signal propagation are omitted. See Ashby (2003) for the fuller relativistic timekeeping problem.

The spatial-slice option embeds the constant-time equatorial exterior geometry in Euclidean 3D:

Z(r)−Z(R)=2rs[r−rs−R−rs],1+(dZdr)2=11−rs/r.Z(r)-Z(R)=2\sqrt{r_s}\left[\sqrt{r-r_s}-\sqrt{R-r_s}\right],\qquad 1+\left(\frac{dZ}{dr}\right)^2=\frac{1}{1-r_s/r}.

Only radii outside the physical body are drawn. The embedding height is magnified by the factor shown on screen; the unscaled geometry obeys the radial metric identity. Z is an embedding coordinate, not a physical downward direction. This depicts a spatial slice, not all of spacetime, and marbles rolling on it would not reproduce geodesics. The older softened potential diagram remains a separately labelled analogy. See the derivation in University of Bath relativity notes.

Tutorial: open Space & Time, select Earth, and choose 3D body, field & clock. Select Earth · 400 km, then Play to follow the ideal circular clock. Compare Earth · 20,200 km and the sign of Gain vs stationary surface. Switch to Schwarzschild spatial slice and read the magnification label. Diagram height only never changes the numerical clock rates. Orbit the 3D view changes the camera, not the physics.

Share the question

Download the two-page project brief and 24-second scientific model animation. The animation is generated from the numerical modules, not recorded from the website. It labels its reference frames, scale changes between shots and illustrative lunar assumptions.

The original question and the 100-light-year preview

The revised two-page brief restores the A-to-B-to-C sightline question, transit-boundary geometry and longer timescales from the original discussion note, which is preserved in full. The original's A, B and C denote observer epochs, unlike the optional synthetic comparison stars in the simulation. The present direct-imaging score experiment does not settle transit-zone crossings for known orbital planes.

100 light-years is a distance, not 100 years. At a constant 233 km/s it takes about 128,666 years. The integrated Solar path includes its 7 km/s initial vertical component and reaches that path length in about 128,608 years. These are model-dependent estimates, not target-encounter forecasts. The idealized orbit is nearly circular in a static smooth axisymmetric potential. Evolution of the Galactic plane is omitted; the animated warp is not coupled to the force model.

Record from the website: click 100 light-years · preview & record, then Preview 10 seconds or Record 10 seconds. The local 3D scene uses equal light-year scales and 10 ly grid spacing; the path covers only about 0.2 degrees around the Galactic centre, so it appears almost straight. Planetary ephemerides are not extrapolated over 129,000 years. The browser records the live scene with its labels and assumptions at 1280 × 720. It saves MP4 where supported, otherwise WebM. Keep the tab visible; hiding it cancels the capture. No audio or external screen content is captured. The earlier 24-second model-rendered animation remains a separate resource.

Illustrated report

The six-page illustrated discussion report follows the original note's visual style, with seven numbered figures, rendered equations, quantitative results, a simulation tutorial and references. It is separate from the two-page brief. Its diagrams and scientific plots are model renderings, not browser screenshots.

18. Coupled relativistic Solar System: the 1PN dynamics lab

The new lab integrates the Sun, eight planetary point masses and the Moon together. Each included body acts on every other included body. A paired Newtonian integration starts from exactly the same state. The relativistic branch uses the order-reduced Einstein–Infeld–Hoffmann first post-Newtonian (1PN) equations, rather than adding only a Solar precession term to prescribed Keplerian orbits. These equations retain corrections of order v2/c2v^2/c^2 and GM/(rc2)GM/(rc^2) in weak fields and slow motion.

This is a coupled relativistic approximation appropriate to this educational Solar System lab. It is not a numerical solution of the full Einstein field equations, a replacement for JPL ephemerides or a spacecraft-navigation product. The GR clock diagrams elsewhere in the project and this dynamical integration have different purposes and assumptions.

Starting data, coordinates and represented bodies

The frozen JPL Horizons queries return geometric barycentric positions and velocities at JD 2461041.5 TDB, labelled 2026.0, with independent comparison states 30 days, one Julian year and ten Julian years later. Coordinates use the J2000 ecliptic orientation with the Solar System barycentre as origin; vectors are uncorrected for light time. Units are AU and AU/day; one AU is 149,597,870.7 km. The input files preserve the request URLs, returned headers, body identifiers and response hashes. The returned planetary states identify DE441 as their source; the model does not claim to reproduce DE441's full force model.

Earth and Moon are separate bodies with separate mass parameters. Mars and the outer planets are represented by their system barycentres and total system mass parameters; their individual satellites are not integrated. Planetary parameters follow the table in Park et al. (2021). Pluto, asteroids and Kuiper-belt objects are omitted. This lab uses Solar System barycentric coordinates; Galactic translation and Galactic tidal forces are not added to these equations or clock rates.

Equations implemented

Let μi=GMi\mu_i=GM_i, dij=ri−rj\mathbf d_{ij}=\mathbf r_i-\mathbf r_j, rij=∣dij∣r_{ij}=|\mathbf d_{ij}|, and define the external positive potential and Newtonian acceleration:

Ui=∑k≠iμkrik,aiN=−∑j≠iμjdijrij3.U_i=\sum_{k\ne i}\frac{\mu_k}{r_{ik}},\qquad \mathbf a_i^N=-\sum_{j\ne i}\frac{\mu_j\mathbf d_{ij}}{r_{ij}^3}.

For GR parameters β=γ=1\beta=\gamma=1, the order-reduced equation used here is:

ai=aiN+1c2∑j≠iμj{dijrij3Aij+dij⋅(4vi−3vj)rij3(vi−vj)+7ajN2rij},\mathbf a_i=\mathbf a_i^N+\frac{1}{c^2}\sum_{j\ne i}\mu_j \left\{\frac{\mathbf d_{ij}}{r_{ij}^3}A_{ij} +\frac{\mathbf d_{ij}\cdot(4\mathbf v_i-3\mathbf v_j)}{r_{ij}^3}(\mathbf v_i-\mathbf v_j) +\frac{7\mathbf a_j^N}{2r_{ij}}\right\},
Aij=4Ui+Uj−vi2−2vj2+4vi⋅vj+32(dij⋅vjrij)2+12dij⋅ajN.A_{ij}=4U_i+U_j-v_i^2-2v_j^2+4\mathbf v_i\cdot\mathbf v_j +\frac{3}{2}\left(\frac{\mathbf d_{ij}\cdot\mathbf v_j}{r_{ij}}\right)^2 +\frac{1}{2}\mathbf d_{ij}\cdot\mathbf a_j^N.

Replacing accelerations inside the 1/c21/c^2 terms by their Newtonian values discards terms beyond the retained 1PN order. This is an explicit order reduction, not an iterative exact-GR solution. The equations follow the published point-mass PPN formulation summarized in Park et al., section 3.1. Tamayo et al. and the REBOUNDx documentation distinguish all-body 1PN dynamics from dominant-central-body approximations. The project's implementation is independently written from the equations; it does not embed REBOUNDx source code.

Fixed-step classical RK4 integrates the velocity-dependent equations. The standard step is 0.0625 day, with 0.03125 day available for refinement. RK4 is not symplectic. The browser computes in a background worker, saves paired states every two days and retains the exact end epoch. Displayed saved states are not precision dense-output ephemerides. The lab accepts spans of 1, 5, 10 or 20 Julian years; the frozen external comparisons extend only to ten years. A longer display span does not imply a validated long-term prediction.

What the checks actually show

The isolated test-particle limit recovers the Schwarzschild weak-field acceleration. A ten-year two-body Mercury test fits the difference of relativistic and Newtonian apsidal angles and returns 42.9798 arcseconds per century, compared with 42.9807 from the analytic 1PN prediction:

Δωorbit=6πGM⊙a(1−e2)c2.\Delta\omega_{\rm orbit}=\frac{6\pi GM_\odot}{a(1-e^2)c^2}.

This is an isolated dynamical benchmark; it is not the full Solar System's total observed precession. At 30 days in the ten-body model, Mercury's heliocentric relativistic/Newtonian position difference is approximately 8.825 km, while halving the integration step changes its relativistic position by 0.000085 km. For the Moon, the same refinement changes the heliocentric position by about 0.00239 km. These are numerical consistency checks, not physical uncertainty bounds.

Body Error vs JPL at 30 days At 1 Julian year At 10 Julian years
Mercury 0.00350 km 0.0666 km 0.324 km
Earth 0.0164 km 0.204 km 1.852 km
Jupiter system 0.00133 km 0.257 km 17.007 km
Moon 1.341 km 17.754 km 215.382 km

Errors are instantaneous heliocentric 3D position discrepancies at the saved epochs, using identical initial states. They do not bound every epoch or every observable. The growing lunar discrepancy reflects omitted physics as well as integration error. Complete results, including all bodies and step-refinement checks, are in data/relativity-validation.json. Additional tests check Newtonian force balance, rotational covariance, 1/c21/c^2 scaling, finite outputs, worker completion and rejection of unsupported settings. No fresh browser rendering or browser-worker execution has been verified in this environment; the worker algorithm is executed directly under Node for validation.

Relative clock rates

The lab gives a separate leading weak-field estimate for ideal nonrotating spherical surface clocks, using each body's centre velocity and external potential, plus its spherical self-potential:

qi=Ui+GMi/Ri+vi2/2c2,dτidt≃1−qi,d(τi−τE)dt≃qE−qi.q_i=\frac{U_i+GM_i/R_i+v_i^2/2}{c^2},\qquad \frac{d\tau_i}{dt}\simeq1-q_i,\qquad \frac{d(\tau_i-\tau_E)}{dt}\simeq q_E-q_i.

The instantaneous readout is microseconds per coordinate day relative to the model Earth clock. The cumulative difference is integrated using trapezoidal quadrature at each dynamics step. It is not a UTC/TT time-transfer solution. Surface rotation, location, tidal potential, atmospheric effects and non-spherical self-gravity are omitted. The Sun's clock, for example, uses its adopted photospheric radius; these readings are not clocks located at singular point-mass centres. The approximation is lower order than a complete relativistic ephemeris/time-transfer treatment; see Ashby (2003).

Light propagation: a limited Solar Shapiro term

For non-occulted Earth-to-body geometry, the optional readout computes the leading one-way delay in the field of a static spherical Sun:

ΔtShapiro=2GM⊙c3ln⁡(rE+rT+RrE+rT−R).\Delta t_{\rm Shapiro}=\frac{2GM_\odot}{c^3}\ln\left(\frac{r_E+r_T+R}{r_E+r_T-R}\right).

Here the endpoints are instantaneous body-centre positions; RR is their geometric separation and rE,rTr_E,r_T are their distances from the Sun. Rays whose straight segment intersects the adopted Solar radius are excluded. This readout is a diagnostic approximation: it omits moving endpoints, retarded positions, light deflection, other bodies' delays and full null-geodesic ray tracing. It does not turn the spatial display into an apparent sky image.

Tutorial and limitations

Open Space & Time → Relativistic Solar System · coupled 1PN lab. Choose a span and integration step, then Calculate both models. When the calculation finishes, press Play or scrub the saved epochs. Use the inner-system, all-planet or Earth–Moon view; drag to orbit and scroll to zoom. Select a readout body to inspect the positional difference, relative surface-clock rate and accumulated clock offset. Export the paired CSV for numerical inspection. The coordinate origin is Sun-centred in the planetary views, at the Solar System barycentre in the all-body barycentric view, and Earth-centred in the lunar view; the integrator itself remains barycentric.

Body markers are enlarged; coordinates use equal AU scales. Grey tracks show the Newtonian comparison. At true scale the relativistic and Newtonian paths mostly overlap: the numerical difference is the useful observable. No artificial precession or difference magnification is silently applied.

The model omits spin/frame dragging, Solar and planetary quadrupoles, other satellites as separate bodies, lunar rotation and tides, asteroids, Pluto, Kuiper-belt perturbations, 2PN and higher corrections, gravitational radiation, a self-consistent evolving spacetime metric and full photon ray tracing. It uses pre-fitted starting data without refitting parameters to observations. These omissions prevent calling it a complete relativistic ephemeris or a full numerical-relativity Solar System. The delivered capability is a reproducible, coupled all-included-body 1PN lab, with measured limits and a Newtonian control.

16. Building a Galaxy from evidence, and separating gas from stars

The current 3D Galaxy replaces the photograph-derived particle layer and filled outer shell with a reproducible synthetic stellar-light model. It is constrained by selected published geometry, not a new fit to the entire Milky Way. There is no external photograph of our Galaxy from this viewpoint.

Static model-input plot, not a screenshot of the browser renderer. The measured catalogue samples only part of the Galaxy.

Measured layer. The frozen Reid et al. (2019) VLBI catalogue supplies 199 parallax entries, with 198 distinct rounded Galactic names. Two entries share G123.06−06.30 and have different aliases and measurements; both are retained. These are high-mass star-forming regions, not a representative census of ordinary stars. Nominal distance is d=1/ϖd=1/\varpi kpc for parallax in mas. The transformation uses the ICRS–Galactic rotation and this project's Sun position (0,−8.2,0.020)(0,-8.2,0.020) kpc. The raw catalogue, references, importer and SHA-256 checksum are included. Positions retain their catalogue epochs; they are not propagated to 2026.

The 168 entries with parallax signal-to-noise at least 5 can show endpoints 1/(ϖ+σϖ)1/(\varpi+\sigma_\varpi) and 1/(ϖ−σϖ)1/(\varpi-\sigma_\varpi). These are transformed measurement-error endpoints, not Bayesian distance intervals. No selection-function or covariance correction is made. This overlay and the published arm segments disappear during future playback rather than masquerading as future observations.

Modelled structure. Six kinked logarithmic arm segments use Table 2 of Reid et al.:

ln⁡(R/Rk)=−(β−βk)tan⁡ψ,(x,y)=(−Rsin⁡β,−Rcos⁡β).\ln(R/R_k)=-(\beta-\beta_k)\tan\psi,\qquad (x,y)=(-R\sin\beta,-R\cos\beta).

The gold fit overlay stops at the published azimuth intervals. The fainter stellar-light continuation extends those fits by 65° at either end (15° for the Local arm): that extension is an illustration, not an observed or uniquely determined arm map. The bar adopts 30° orientation and 5 kpc half-length, consistent with Wegg, Gerhard & Portail (2015), without refitting their data.

The 190,000 samples represent synthetic light, not individual measured stars. For the natural-light view, their projected disk/bar/arm distributions are smoothed into a 384×384 density map, with analytic vertical profiles. A 112-step volume renderer integrates illustrative emission and absorption through this 3D distribution; a bounded exposure transform prevents a saturated white centre. About 6,130 faint point sources add depth cues. Dust lanes, emissivity, opacity and colour are presentation assumptions, not calibrated photometry or a fitted extinction map. A subdued 180° counterpart of the arm-light map supplies an illustrative two-fold continuation on the poorly constrained far side; it is not measured structure and does not modify the published arm-fit overlay. Measurement markers are off by default and remain available through the evidence controls. Sampling weights are 56% smooth disk, 22% bar and 22% arm component before radius/height rejection. The disk has an adopted 2.6 kpc radial scale and 0.3/0.9 kpc vertical scales; arm colours, clumping, extensions, relative weights, flaring, dust dimming and luminosities are display assumptions. They do not measure stellar density, drive the gravitational potential or predict star formation. The separate environment panel retains its explicitly assumed density model. The kinematic warp uses the existing sourced 700 pc scale at 14 kpc; it is not a fit to the 2025 corrugation. Default vertical scale is 1×; Show warped disk selects labelled 5× and a suitable camera.

A real, limited hydrodynamics experiment

Gas hydrodynamics lab solves the two-dimensional, isothermal Euler equations in a prescribed potential. The 3D surface height represents gas surface density, not the vertical shape of a three-dimensional gas disk:

∂tΣ+∇⋅(Σu)=0,∂t(Σu)+∇⋅(Σu⊗u+cs2ΣI)=−Σ∇Φ.\partial_t\Sigma+\nabla\cdot(\Sigma\mathbf u)=0, \qquad \partial_t(\Sigma\mathbf u)+\nabla\cdot(\Sigma\mathbf u\otimes\mathbf u+c_s^2\Sigma\mathbf I)=-\Sigma\nabla\Phi.
Φ=12vc2ln⁡[(R2+rc2)/rc2]+ϵvc2b2(x2−y2)cos⁡2α+2xysin⁡2α(R2+b2)2.\Phi=\tfrac12 v_c^2\ln[(R^2+r_c^2)/r_c^2] +\epsilon v_c^2 b^2\frac{(x^2-y^2)\cos2\alpha+2xy\sin2\alpha}{(R^2+b^2)^2}.

Here rc=1r_c=1 kpc, b=5b=5 kpc, vc=233v_c=233 km/s, cs=10c_s=10 km/s, ϵ=0.1\epsilon=0.1, and α=−Ωbt\alpha=-\Omega_b t with Ωb=40\Omega_b=40 km/s/kpc. The bar and initial gas rotate in the same clockwise direction in the displayed coordinates. The initial surface density is proportional to exp⁡(−R/4 kpc)\exp(-R/4\,{\rm kpc}), with circular speed including its radial pressure gradient in the axisymmetric potential. The bar perturbation is present from the start; the initial state is not an equilibrium with the bar.

Implementation: 64×64 cells over 32×32 kpc, first-order finite-volume Rusanov flux, gravity kicks bracketing the flux update, Courant factor 0.3, and zero-gradient open boundaries. The boundary flux is included in the mass budget. Density is never silently clipped. The independent gas clock runs to 100 Myr; Export gas grid supplies positions, density and velocities. Top view and 3D density view change the camera only.

The isothermal closure exchanges heat implicitly and does not evolve an energy equation; compare the standard hydrodynamics equations documented for Athena. This project uses its own much simpler implementation, not Athena. It omits magnetic fields, self-gravity, cooling physics, feedback, star formation and an observational gas fit. It is numerically diffusive and is not a validated hydrodynamic reconstruction of the Milky Way. The stellar orbits, Solar System and heliosphere are not driven by this gas experiment. A credible heliosphere flow calculation would additionally require magnetohydrodynamics and interstellar-plasma boundary data.

Tests preserve uniform gas exactly, conserve periodic mass, account for open-boundary mass flux, compare acceleration with the potential gradient, and recover a small-amplitude travelling acoustic wave with decreasing error on grid refinement. These verify limited numerical behaviour, not astrophysical realism. Stars and planets continue to use gravitational trajectories; fluid equations are not used to produce attractive but unphysical corkscrews.

17. What changes after 100, 1,000 and 10,000 years?

Years after 2026 Solar path (ly) Median sightline shift (arcsec) Median absolute distance change Change in accessibility sum
100 0.0777 44.4 0.0126% 0.009111 (0.0307%)
1,000 0.7772 443.9 0.1257% 0.083706 (0.2825%)
10,000 7.7720 4461.9 1.2621% 0.505789 (1.7069%)

Scores use the same hypothetical 1 AU, Earth-radius planet distribution and baseline 60 mas / 10⁻¹⁰ contrast / G=30 thresholds. They are not discovery counts.

The Solar path column assumes constant tangential speed 233 km/s on a locally circular Galactic path. Over 10,000 years it covers about 7.77 light-years and 0.01665° around the centre: still the local Galactic neighbourhood, not a journey into a different spiral arm. The gas clock and the 250 Myr context view answer different questions.

Sightline angles come from the relative three-dimensional motion of the same 1,387 selected Gaia DR3 sources, propagated from their catalogue epochs to 2026 and then to the comparison year:

qi(t)=qi(t0)+vi,rel(t−t0),Δθi=atan2⁡(∣qi(t0)×qi(t)∣,qi(t0)⋅qi(t)).\mathbf q_i(t)=\mathbf q_i(t_0)+\mathbf v_{i,\mathrm{rel}}(t-t_0),\qquad \Delta\theta_i=\operatorname{atan2}(|\mathbf q_i(t_0)\times\mathbf q_i(t)|,\mathbf q_i(t_0)\cdot\mathbf q_i(t)).

This is a nominal screening calculation, not a certified 10,000-year ephemeris. Constant velocity omits Galactic differential acceleration, binary dynamics and observer orbital parallax. Uncertainties are not newly propagated for the 1,000- and 10,000-year rows; the earlier century experiment separately provides formal astrometric uncertainty. Gaia quality cuts, available radial velocities and the fixed sample introduce selection effects. Sources not in this sample are not counted as future entrants.

Changing sightlines can open or close a transit window. But the isotropic planet population in this direct-imaging calculation marginalises over orbital orientation: its score changes through distance, brightness and angular-separation thresholds, not through the plotted sky angle itself. Identifying new transits requires orbital planes and their uncertainties for individual systems. Kaltenegger & Faherty (2021) already demonstrated time-dependent membership of Earth's transit zone. This project does not claim that changing viewpoints are an undiscovered idea.

Closer systems can make imaging and spectroscopy easier; they can also have less favourable orbital phase or obscuring dust. Nothing in these calculations establishes life, a new habitable planet or a future discovery count. A useful next experiment would rank individual targets at fixed exposure time and instrument performance, propagate binary and astrometric uncertainties, and test whether any gains survive. A second observer needs a feasible spacecraft trajectory: a released probe retains its initial velocity and does not remain at a fixed Galactic location.

How to inspect the new layers

  1. Open Milky Way → Inspect the measured evidence. Cyan points are catalogue entries, cyan segments show the selected distance-error endpoints, and gold curves show published arm segments. Rotate/zoom to inspect them.
  2. Select Natural stellar light to restore synthetic light; use Show warped disk for the bend and compare labelled 1×/5× vertical scales. Turn off Keep bend in view before choosing your own camera.
  3. Open Gas hydrodynamics lab, play its independent clock, compare top and density views, and export the cell values. Density-height is a graph, not a warped Galactic surface.
  4. In the report's 100 / 1,000 / 10,000 year comparison, select an interval. Read distance and sightline changes separately from the conditional accessibility score. The Solar System century clock is deliberately not extended beyond its ephemeris domain.
